title.en: He-Goes-to-Listen: The Scarred Nephew and the Singing Wives
title.zh: 赴聽者：帶疤的姪兒與歌聲之妻

region.en: Hill by the Genesee River, Tonawanda Seneca country, New York
region.zh: 紐約州托納萬達塞內卡地區傑納西河畔的山丘

texts.period: Related almost verbatim by Gohweh, an old Tonawanda Seneca (Parker 1923)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 12, 'He-Goes-to-Listen' (1923)

summary.en: An old widower uncle maims and scars his nephew Hatondas so he can claim the two singing women foretold by the boy's mother's dream. The women arrive, reject the trickster, and take Hatondas; crawling through a hollow log transforms him into a handsome man, but his broken silence-taboo costs him one of his three magic bags. Years later he returns with presents, and the uncle, now welcoming, jokes his way out of an axe-beard before the lodge renews itself.
summary.zh: 老鰥夫叔叔為奪取姪兒母親夢中預言的兩位歌女，刻意毀傷其容貌。歌女們抵達後識破詭計，選擇了哈頓達斯；鑽過空心圓木使他蛻變為俊美男子，但他破壞了緘默禁忌，失去三只法袋之一。多年後他攜禮而歸，叔叔笑言相迎，木屋亦煥然如新。

sensitivity.note: Tonawanda Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Cruelty to the boy is folktale register.

passages.text: Near a large hill that rose from a river lived a boy named Hatondas - He-Goes-to-Listen - his name bestowed because just before his birth his mother had dreamed that at marriageable age two singing women would come from afar to be his wives, and that she would die. She sewed three witched bags, one filled with wampum, one with beautiful clothing, one left empty, each able to hold things hundreds of times its size. Her widower brother-in-law, unable to secure a wife by fair means, resolved to disfigure the boy and claim the women himself; day after day he threw hot embers on the boy and stretched a deer tendon across the doorway so he would fall, until the once-handsome child was scarred and crippled.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 116-118; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the boy's seventeenth year he returned from the hill in great excitement: he had heard singing. The uncle, suppressing his own excitement, beat him brutally and threw him into the fire, then oiled and painted his own face, tied his flabby cheeks back with sinews, and let down his black hair to hide the ruse. That night the women came, sat on Hatondas' low bench, and would only ask, 'Where is Hatondas?' - knocking the old reprobate down when he pleaded. Hatondas returned suddenly bold, and the two women cooked his supper while the old man fared as best he could.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 118-119; not verbatim.

passages.text: That night the uncle's heart changed. He filled the empty bag with parched corn, maple sugar, a bow, arrows and a buckskin suit, and warned Hatondas not to speak to any living creature but his wives, on pain of losing a bag. On the hilltop one of the women pointed to a hollow log; crawling through it, Hatondas emerged smooth-faced, unscarred and clad in white skin - but in his delight he spoke to two strangers, and the wampum bag vanished, so he entered the strange country as a common man. Years later he returned with presents for the old uncle, and after their bargaining joke the lodge renewed itself while the old man grew older.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 120-122; not verbatim.

title.en: Hatondas the Listener Finds a Wife

region.en: Cattaraugus Seneca Reservation, New York (collection pin)
region.zh: 紐約州卡塔勞格斯塞內卡保留地（採集定位）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 13, 'Hahtondas, the Listener, Finds a Wife' (1923)

summary.en: A cruel uncle sends his abused orphan up the hill to listen until he hears a new sound; the sound is a woman singing his name. She cleans him with hot oil, transforms him through a hollow log, and burns the lodge as the uncle attacks; she beats a tiny bundle into a growing dog they ride to the lake, where the monstrous bear Nia-gwa-he fishes for their canoe with a living line, drinks the lake dry, freezes it, and is sunk by steaming water. On the cliff her sister welcomes them, and their precocious twin sons hurl the returning monster into an oak grove.
summary.zh: 殘忍的叔叔命飽受虐待的孤兒上山傾聽，直到聽見新的聲音；那聲音是一位女子唱著他的名字。她以熱油為他淨身，引他穿空心圓木蛻變，並縱火燒屋以逃；她將小皮束抽打成漸大的犬，騎至湖邊。巨熊尼亞瓜赫以活索釣舟、吸乾湖水、冰封湖面，終被滾水沉入湖底。崖頂的姐姐迎接二人，其早慧的雙生子最後將再來的怪物拋入橡樹林。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Jimerson informant, Parker 1923); public domain. Parker notes it is apparently a mixture of two distinct legends.

passages.text: Hatondas was a poor orphan who lived with a wrinkled old uncle who threw hot coals at him and mutilated him. Ordered up the hill to listen until he heard a sound he had never heard, he reported owl, hawk, woodpecker, deer and bear, and was beaten for each. At last he heard a song calling his own name: 'Hatondas, Hatondas, I am coming to marry you now.' The uncle washed and dressed himself and claimed the bride, but the young woman said, 'He is the man I have come to marry,' cleaned the boy's head of crusts with heated oil, and led him to a hollow log through which he emerged clean and healed of his scars.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 122-124; not verbatim.

passages.text: At midnight a queer sound awoke them. 'He is upon us!' she cried, scattering embers so the lodge caught fire. On the hilltop she struck a tiny bundle with a whip: a growl became a dog that grew with every stroke until both could mount its back and dash away. On the shore of a vast water they took a canoe, but a gigantic bear cast a long fish line that wrapped the stern and began hauling them in. 'Empty your pipe on the line' - it snapped. The monster swallowed water in such quantities that the lake changed its current toward his mouth, until the young woman threw a round white stone into his belly, and he belched the waters back.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 124-126; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'You cannot escape me. I am Nia-gwa-he!' the bear roared, blowing icy breath until the lake froze and he galloped out over the surface. The canoe stood fast in the ice, but the wife knelt by her little fire and flung a kettle of steaming water at his feet; the ice softened, the monster sank and disappeared. The canoe grated at the foot of a high cliff, where a woman dropped down two pairs of claw mittens, and her sister greeted the bridal pair. A year later the wife bore twin boys who felled two intruders at their birth and grew within hours into men of prodigious strength; when Nia-gwa-he returned looking like a buffalo, they wrapped their arms around it and threw it through the air into a grove of oaks, and buried it there.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 126-127; not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of the Chestnut Tree

region.en: Land of hills eastward (symbolic pin at Allegheny hills, New York-Pennsylvania border)
region.zh: 東方丘陵之地（象徵性定位於紐約與賓州交界之阿利根尼丘陵）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 14, 'The Origin of the Chestnut Tree' (1923)

summary.en: Dadjedondji secretly watches his brother Hawiyas cook a magic pudding from one small nut, boils the whole bag himself, and is told the food is charmed and unobtainable - beyond a chasm, a poisonous serpent, two panthers and a flayed witch whose look makes men fall apart. Dadjedondji goes east with wooden dolls for the guardians, stops the singing skin-woman's mouth with wampum that chokes her silent, receives the nuts from her six grateful cannibal sisters, rebukes the freed monsters, closes the chasm, and scatters the chestnuts over the hills - whose powers are gone.
summary.zh: 達杰東吉偷看兄長哈維亞斯以一顆小堅果煮出魔法布丁，自己也煮了整袋，卻被告知此物受咒、常人不可得——其東有裂谷、毒蛇、雙豹與一位目光令人碎裂的剝皮巫女。達杰東吉攜木偶東行：以貝珠堵住皮女歌口致其窒息，受六位感恩的食人姊妹贈堅果，訓誡解脫的怪物，合攏裂谷，並將栗子撒遍丘陵——但其魔力已然消散。

sensitivity.note: Seneca aition (Parker 1923); public domain. Wampum as the emblem of truth is a distinctly Iroquoian moral device.

passages.text: In a lodge in a land of hills lived Dadjedondji with his older brother Hawiyas, who never ate in anyone's presence but smoked all day. Watching secretly, Dadjedondji saw his brother scrape shavings from a small nut into a kettle of water that swelled as it heated until a pudding was cooked. The next night the boy boiled the entire bag, and the kettle expanded until it filled half the house. 'Oh what have you done?' cried Hawiyas. 'You have used all my food. No one can obtain more of its kind, for it is far away and charmed, so you have killed your brother!'
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 128-130; not verbatim.

passages.text: The brother told the history: to the east was a great gap in the earth; beyond, a monstrous serpent whose poisonous breath killed all that came; beyond, two panthers; and high in the tree that bore the wonderful nuts, a witch whose very look made men fall apart, her six sisters devouring their meat. Dadjedondji reasoned that these things were not right and therefore could be conquered. He whittled wooden dolls and threw one across the chasm, following it with a running jump; flung one into the serpent's jaws and one into each panther's mouth; and at the great tree found the singer to be a flayed human skin, whose charm song had no effect on him.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 130-131; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Come down here, I have a present for you - gaswe'nda, wampum,' he called, and the skin-woman descended. Holding the necklace she sang, 'I have been bribed by a present of wampum not to tell of a stranger's approach,' and as the beads grew tight they choked her into silence. Out rushed the six sisters, their cries not of anger but glad joy, thanking him for rescuing them from their evil sister. They gave him a great bag of brown nuts; the great witch, left without food, perished. Dadjedondji rebuked the panthers, sent the serpent wriggling to the nearest lake, and commanded the chasm: 'Close up once again and let men enjoy themselves!' - and the earth closed with a loud crash.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 131-132; not verbatim.

passages.text: He sent his brother to the six sisters to find a wife, then scattered the nuts over the hills; in time beautiful trees grew, and now all the world has chestnuts. When they were confined to one tree they were magical, but now their powers have gone, and they neither spread nor burst kettles.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, p. 132; not verbatim.

title.en: Divided Body Rescues a Girl from a Wizard's Island
title.zh: 分體者自巫師之島救回少女

region.en: Island in a large lake (symbolic pin in Lake Ontario offshore, New York)
region.zh: 大湖中的島嶼（象徵性定位於紐約州安大略湖上）

source.archive: Internet Archive (Buffalo Historical Society Publications, vol. 27)
source.work: A. C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, ch. V tale 15, 'Divided Body Rescues a Girl from a Wizard's Island' (1923)

summary.en: A girl who disobeys her brother is snatched by the hair to the island of the cannibal wizard Ohgwe'Ias, where she must cook human flesh. The half-bodied helper Sgagedi, the Other Side, coaches her to dodge the wizard's club, paddles from both ends of his split body, counters the wizard's wind charm with tobacco, and reunites at the landing; their twins later find the girl's grief-mad brother, restore his petrified dog, and bring the whole family together.
summary.zh: 少女違逆兄長出門取水，被髮絲拽往食人巫師歐格威之島，被迫烹煮人肉。半身助者「另一側」教她閃避巫師之棒，以分開的半身划槳，以菸草反制巫師的風咒，登岸時軀體合而為一。其雙生子後來尋得悲傷成疾的舅舅，使化為石頭的犬復生，闔家團圓。

sensitivity.note: Seneca tale (Parker 1923); public domain. Cannibal-wizard Ohgwe'Ias is a stock Seneca ogre.

passages.text: A brother and younger sister dwelt together, the brother Crow hunting and the sister cooking; he never allowed her to leave the lodge, even for the spring, setting his dog as guard. One morning she debated why she should be kept within and pushed aside the curtain - 'Now I shall see!' - and as she dipped water something grabbed her by the hair and whisked her through the air to an island in a large lake, where human bones lay gnawed about a great lodge. She knew she had been abducted by a cannibal wizard, Ohgwe'Ias, and each morning he brought human flesh and demanded she prepare it.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 133-134; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the spring she met a pleasant young man who warned her: tomorrow the wizard will strike at you as you reach for the bowl - jump behind the post, he will hit the pole and break his arm; then run. So it happened, and she fled to the canoe. Sgagedi, the Other Side, shoved the canoe from the beach, throwing one half of his body to the bow and leaving one-half at the stern, paddling from both ends and going very rapidly. Ohgwe'Ias sang a charm song calling the winds to blow the canoe back, and it swept toward the island - but Sgagedi threw tobacco on the water and called on the wind to blow the other way, and the canoe grounded safe on the opposite shore, where his body came together with a snap.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 134-135; not verbatim.

passages.text: An elderly woman met them on the forest path: 'I have been waiting for you to become my daughter-in-law.' But the bride could not be happy, continually crying, 'Oh where is my brother?' When Crow had returned to find her gone he had scolded the dog until it turned into a smooth stone. In due season the sister bore twin sons who grew quickly; they paddled across the lake, followed an old streak in the sky inland, and pulled a breathing body from a fallen bark lodge. 'I am your uncle,' said the old man. 'My dog is a stone. Oh, will you restore my dog to life!' The twins restored the dog, and when the sister saw her brother she knew him and was very glad.
passages.note: Condensed from Parker 1923, pp. 135-136; not verbatim.
